findings.title: Concurrent writes and file lock staleness create data corruption risk in shared artifact store
findings.summary: Multiple concurrent orchestrator runs share `.audit-tools/audit/` artifacts (audit_state.json, artifact_metadata.json, findings). Three related mechanisms are broken: (1) File lock staleness detection uses mtime with a 30-second window, fragile under filesystem variance, clock skew, and GC pauses (P5-DR-001); (2) Concurrent artifact writes lack explicit ordering guarantees — Run A and B can simultaneously hold locks on different files and corrupt the global artifact bundle (P5-DR-002); (3) Lock heartbeat refresh silently fails without surfacing errors, allowing a holder to lose its lock mid-operation (P5-DR-011). While each file write is individually atomic, the staleness cascade (staleness.ts) assumes a single writer during the whole dependency-based recomputation. A write-ordering race is possible where Run A computes staleness against metadata_v1, Run B writes metadata_v2, and Run A writes findings_v1 based on stale metadata, silently overwriting Run B's findings. The design philosophy demands tool-enforced guarantees, never host discretion; this leaks to the host.

findings.title: Contract-pipeline artifact reading bypasses version validation entirely
findings.summary: The readContractArtifact() function in src/remediate/contractPipeline/artifactStore.ts (line 310-319) reads JSON envelopes with zero validation of the contract_version field. It returns raw, unvalidated envelopes that may have mismatched or missing contract_version values. The contract-pipeline architecture's staleness DAG depends on version matching for semantic stability, yet there is no enforcement when reading from disk. Dependent code in detectStaleArtifacts() assumes envelope.dependency_hashes and envelope.payload are present and well-formed (lines 366-367, 210), creating cascading failures if the file is corrupted or manually edited. A manually edited artifact with an incorrect contract_version would silently propagate staleness calculation errors and potentially cause downstreams to incorrectly treat valid artifacts as stale.

findings.title: RemediationBlock.touched_files validation is type-unsafe despite required field
findings.summary: In src/remediate/validation/remediationState.ts, validateRemediationBlock() declares touched_files as a required key (line 94 via requireKeys), but the type validation (lines 109-119) only runs when value.touched_files !== undefined. This creates a contract violation window: a block with touched_files: null would pass requireKeys (which checks 'in value' semantics, true for null values) but skip the array type check. The result could pass validation with null, number, string, or any non-array value. The file-ownership scheduler and attributePostMergeFailure both expect touched_files to be a string array, making this a correctness gap that could cause runtime crashes or silent data corruption when invalid blocks reach the scheduler.

findings.title: Schema version mismatch handling trades silent data loss for safety — categorization is made at every callsite
findings.summary: The schema mismatch policy (schemaVersion.ts) treats regenerable state differently from costly state: regenerable is silently discarded, costly throws. This is correct in principle but broken in practice: the categorization is made by each caller independently (dozens of places), there is no central registry of which artifacts are regenerable vs costly, and no validation that the categorization is consistent. If a critical artifact (a user confirmation, an LLM-authored finding, an external-analyzer result) is mistakenly treated as regenerable, a schema upgrade will silently drop it without recovery. Conversely, if a derived cache is treated as costly, a schema upgrade blocks the run. The burden falls entirely on developers. Additionally, when artifact_metadata.json has an old schema version, computeStaleArtifacts immediately marks ALL DAG artifacts as stale and re-runs from scratch — a conservative fail-safe for safety but wasteful and prone to quota burnout if a schema extension (not breaking change) triggers an all-stale cascade across a fleet of workers. Corroborated by P5-DR-003 (schema version mismatch) and P5-DR-004 (metadata migration fallback).

findings.title: 28-obligation priority chain creates steep iteration friction; obligation engine and state machines remain implicit
findings.summary: The audit orchestrator's PRIORITY array contains 28 sequential obligations (repo_manifest → … → friction_capture_current). Each obligation has its own executor, state derivation, staleness tracking, and test coverage. Adding a new capability or refining an existing one requires: (1) creating/modifying an executor + executor runner; (2) inserting into the priority chain (risking cascading staleness recalculation); (3) writing happy-path and error-path tests; (4) updating backlog/memory. The backlog documents repeated incidents (CP-NODE-4, DD-9) where a new obligation or mid-chain refactor cost more in downstream debugging than initial work. Pragmatically, this is sound architecture — it PREVENTS bugs by forcing every step explicit — but the cost to iterate is high (P1-DR-001). Related: the obligation engine (scan, fold logic) and the drain-fold-halt model (deterministic steps fold silently, operator-interactive breaks the fold) are load-bearing design choices but entirely implicit — zero inline documentation explaining the model or when steps fold vs halt (P3-DR-006). The remediate state machine (pending → planning → implementing → closing → complete, with side-branches) is likewise embedded in conditional logic across multiple files, not declared as data (P2-DR-006, P3-DR-008). Neither orchestrator represents its state machine topology as a first-class artifact; the obligation-to-executor coupling is dual-sourced (PRIORITY array + EXECUTOR_REGISTRY, maintained in sync) (P2-DR-001). These are interconnected design choices, all visible when one person needs to add or refine a capability. A pragmatist would ask: could a smaller core chain (10-12 obligation classes) with internal state machines (phases inside ONE obligation) cut iteration friction without sacrificing safety? Could the obligation engine be documented and state machines represented as data? Corroborated by P1-DR-001, P2-DR-001, P2-DR-006, P3-DR-006, P3-DR-008.

findings.title: Case-sensitive file extension check misses uppercase .CMD and .PS1 files on Windows
findings.summary: The Windows shell-wrapping logic uses case-sensitive `endsWith()` checks for '.cmd' and '.ps1' extensions, but Windows file extensions are case-insensitive. Commands like 'FOO.CMD' would not be wrapped in cmd.exe.

findings.title: Circular dependencies indicate misplaced abstraction boundaries in quota, remediate contract pipeline, and state/status
findings.summary: Three circular dependencies are documented: (1) src/shared/quota/limits.ts ↔ scheduler.ts (quota rate-limiting model interdependent with scheduling); (2) src/remediate/contractPipeline/artifactStore.ts ↔ semanticProjection.ts (artifact storage depends on semantic logic, which depends back on storage); (3) src/remediate/state/types.ts ↔ itemStatus.ts (state types depend on item status, vice versa). Each cycle signals a missing abstraction: two modules that need to reference each other likely define concepts that should be co-located or extracted into a third module (P2-DR-008, P5-DR-008). Cycles complicate testing (mocking requires breaking the cycle), complicate refactoring (code movement must preserve the cycle), hide true data flow, and create initialization-order hazards (if either module relies on side effects during module load, the import order determines behavior). A cleaner design would eliminate cycles by identifying the upstream/downstream relationship and ensuring dependency flows in one direction. For the quota example: scheduler and limits should be orthogonal (scheduler decides WHEN work attempts, limits decide HOW MUCH work allowed), but instead are interdependent. Corroborated by P2-DR-008, P5-DR-008.

findings.title: Deterministic graph extraction prioritizes completeness over accuracy; leads get promoted to findings without semantic gate
findings.summary: The audit pipeline extracts a dependency graph deterministically using multiple analyzers (ast-grep, tree-sitter, manifest parsers). The design philosophy says this output is LEADS, not verdicts — subject to semantic confirmation. But this is breaking in practice. Generic cut-edge detection labels ordinary test/asset/manifest bridges as systemic fragility without semantic separation; absolute co-change counts in git history overstate impact of broad migrations; whole-document file co-mentions masquerade as declared module boundaries (P1-DR-004). These leads get promoted to findings without a confirmed semantic boundary. The design has a semantic review step in the pipeline (design_assessment, charter extraction) that COULD be the confirmation boundary, but it runs downstream and doesn't wire back to reject graph-only findings. There's no mechanical gate preventing a lead from becoming a finding; the tool is shipping findings with dubious provenance. A pragmatist would suggest: either (a) exclude test/asset/manifest edges from the starting graph, or (b) require that a graph-derived finding cite an explicit semantic confirmation (a documented risk reason, an interdependency) before promotion. This would reduce noise and make remediation more actionable.

findings.title: External analyzer acquisition and dispatch packet validation lack explicit error escalation
findings.summary: Two silent-failure chokepoints exist: (1) External analyzer acquisition (acquisitionEngine.ts) has no escalation policy when binary unavailable (network error, checksum mismatch, npx missing). The tool degrades to empty results (marked 'skipped') and continues with degraded signal, silently producing a low-quality audit under adverse conditions (P5-DR-006). (2) Dispatch packet merge (merge-results.mjs) does not validate packet schema before persisting. If a worker emits malformed JSON (missing required field, wrong type), it passes merge-validation as long as task_id is present, and is written to persistent results. Downstream ingestion then processes corrupted data, cascading error into audit_state.json (P5-DR-012). Both are correct for fail-closed (they don't crash), but neither signals that the run is degraded. On a system with transient tool unavailability or network issues, a run might proceed with no external analyzers running or with corrupted results, indistinguishable from a normal run. More correct design: validate packet schema eagerly before persisting, escalate missing-tool status per run configuration (required vs optional tool), make degradation visible in the findings report.

findings.title: LOCK_TIMEOUT_MARGIN_MS contract assumes constant HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL_MS and STALE_LOCK_MS relationship
findings.summary: In src/shared/quota/fileLock.ts and src/shared/io/lockedJsonStore.ts, the lock timeout contract depends on a precise mathematical relationship: HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL_MS (10s = STALE_LOCK_MS/3) and LOCK_TIMEOUT_MARGIN_MS (10s) are hardcoded as independent constants. The lockedJsonStore contract states: 'a fresh-but-held lock then times out deterministically before it could be reclaimed as stale'. However, the heartbeat interval and margin are single-sourced nowhere; if either constant drifts independent of the other, or if the relationship between STALE_LOCK_MS and HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL_MS changes, the invariant breaks silently. A slow-running critical section that takes 27 seconds would be declared stale after 30s while the heartbeat (which runs every 10s) might still be running, violating INV-SCC-08. The contract is unenforced and must be mechanically validated.

findings.title: Metadata schema migration fallback cascades re-computation without bounds; quota burnout risk with incremental deploys
findings.summary: When artifact_metadata.json has an old schema version, computeStaleArtifacts immediately marks ALL present DAG artifacts as stale and re-runs from scratch. This is conservative but does not distinguish between (a) truly incompatible schema vs (b) schema extension that adds optional fields old readers ignore. A minor version bump (1.0 → 1.1 with only new optional fields) triggers the same all-stale cascade (P5-DR-004). This is correct for safety but wasteful. More critically: if the tool is deployed incrementally across workers and a newer auditor produces metadata an older auditor cannot parse, the older auditor will cascade-re-run on every invocation, burning quota indefinitely until all workers are updated. A smarter policy: (1) distinguish major vs minor version mismatches, (2) attempt incremental recovery for minor version deltas, (3) escalate an error with recovery instructions when a genuinely incompatible schema is encountered, rather than silently re-running forever.

findings.title: OpenCode loader omits the mandatory capability handshake
findings.summary: The installed OpenCode command tells the host to make bare next-step calls on every iteration. The canonical loader contract requires an --auditor capability handshake on every call; without authoritative limits, packet sizing pauses, so a fresh OpenCode invocation cannot advance to review dispatch.

affected_files.quoted_text:
Use `audit-code next-step` as the primary interface to the audit workflow.

1. Run `audit-code next-step` directly when shell access is available.
2. Read `prompt_content` in the response and follow it.
3. When a step completes (not blocked), run `audit-code next-step` again.

After `audit-code ensure --quiet` bootstraps the repository, ask the backend for
exactly one next step. This is also the **capability handshake**: report what you
can dispatch to *right now* on every `next-step` call so the backend sizes review
packets against reported or configured limits. When no authoritative limits are
available, capacity remains unknown and packet sizing pauses.

findings.title: Orchestrators share one core in philosophy but have already diverged in implementation; 'one core, two draws' is aspirational
findings.summary: The design philosophy states 'One core, two draws' — a shared obligation engine in src/shared, with audit-code and remediate-code each selecting which obligations matter to them. The shared code exists (advance, obligation engine, graph types, quota subsystem), but the two orchestrators have already diverged in their step logic, state machines, and dispatch strategies. Audit has 28 priorities and MAX_DRAIN_STEPS=64; remediate has a different state machine (pending → planning → implementing → closing → complete) and its own dispatch/phase orchestration. The shared obligation machinery is thin — mostly type definitions and `findFirstActionableObligation` scan. Each orchestrator has ~200 files of domain-specific code that looks similar but isn't unified. The shared obligation machinery is NOT mechanically enforced (no shared trait, no common base class), so drift is silent. The quota subsystem is duplicated in each (both have their own `providers/` + `quota/` wiring) despite SHARED claiming to own them. When a third orchestrator is added (a live possibility per project memory), the reuse question becomes critical — copy-paste the orchestrator structure, or refactor the core to be more reusable? The CLAUDE.md says 'differences between audit and remediate are policy axes of the shared core, almost never a reason to fork it' — but the current state is closer to two loosely-coordinated subsystems than one core with two policies (P1-DR-003). This matters because: (1) a bug fix or feature in one often belongs in both, but the boundary is not mechanically enforced; (2) quota logic is fragmented; (3) divergence under ongoing development is inevitable. It's not broken, but it's not as tight as it claims to be. Pragmatically: would it be healthier to admit that or to actually achieve the unified core? Corroborated by P1-DR-003, P2-DR-005.

findings.title: Provider dispatch routing is a complex multi-layer system; stratification is implicit and unclear which layer wins
findings.summary: The provider factory (src/shared/providers/providerFactory.ts) implements a complex priority table (PROVIDER_PRIORITY_RULES) with 12 ranked rules to choose among 9+ provider backends (opencode, codex, agy, vscode-task, antigravity, subprocess-template, openai-compatible, worker-command, claude-worker). Each rule is an environment/config predicate. This stratifies poorly: the rules mix orthogonal concerns (IDE detection, CLI availability, config presence, in-session markers) into a single priority sequence, making composition impossible — the order matters in ways that are implicit (P2-DR-002). Provider dispatch also splits across multiple layers: (1) host provider auto-resolution (detectHostDispatchWall); (2) provider capability matching (classifyProvider); (3) quota-aware tier selection (dispatch pool bucketing); (4) runtime learned limits (429/524/TPM/RPM parsing); (5) failure recovery (admitSpawn, failover) (P1-DR-009). When routing decisions go wrong, debugging is hard because the decision logic scatters across five files and two orchestrators. The memory index notes this is a known problem ("unified dispatch routing direction") but hasn't shipped. For users, this manifests as dispatch grinding to a halt when a quota hits and fallback isn't configured right, or work landing on slow/weak models when better ones are available (P5-DR-005 — provider dispatch silently degrades on invalid host model roster). Additionally, dispatch logic is duplicated across audit (925 lines in src/audit/cli/dispatch.ts) and remediate (144 lines in src/remediate/steps/dispatch.ts) (P2-DR-005), both solving similar problems independently. Corroborated by P1-DR-009, P2-DR-002, P2-DR-005, P3-DR-009.

findings.title: Remediation accept/claim/merge cycle is complex; failures leave stale worktrees and unreliable state transitions
findings.summary: Remediate's implement phase has a complex state machine: accept node → claim work → dispatch to provider/worktree → merge results → release claim. When a provider fails mid-work or network interruption happens, state gets stuck: the node is accepted, the claim is held (bounded by a lease), the worktree persists, merge hasn't run (P1-DR-007). The backlog documents this explicitly ('Remediation pause/recovery is not durable') — a plan-only stop left state.json at status:implementing with stale worktrees. There's no mechanical guarantee that a pause is resumable or that cleanup happens automatically. Additionally, remediate dispatch has no explicit midway-failure recovery or rollback — if a wave fails partway (10 of 15 tasks succeed), successful changes are committed locally, failed changes marked in state machine, and the run continues. A later phase failure leaves committed work in orphaned worktrees (P5-DR-007). The current code has a grace period (lease timeout), but there's no guarantee that a paused run is distinguishable from a crashed run. The tool tries to be too clever about preserving state across interruptions. Would it be simpler to use git worktrees themselves as the source of truth for liveness (does the worktree still exist? uncommitted work?) rather than a separate lease/claim file? Or to automatically clean up on close-out and require explicit `resume` to pick up where a plan-only stop left off? Corroborated by P1-DR-007, P5-DR-007.

findings.title: State persistence should route through unified AtomicStateStore in shared
findings.summary: Audit writes artifacts directly via writeJsonFile (non-atomic), while remediate uses LockedJsonStore with atomic temp→rename. findings.title: Topological sort in circular-dependency detection incomplete — only processes nodes reachable from zero-degree sources
findings.summary: The circular-obligation-dependency detection at lines 165-221 uses Kahn's topological sort algorithm to find cycles, but the implementation has a subtle incompleteness: it only processes nodes discovered via the queue (zero-degree starts + their descendants). If there exists a cycle that is not reachable from any zero-in-degree node (e.g., a pure cycle with no external dependencies), the queue will empty before processing any cycle member, and visited will be less than ids.size. However, the algorithm correctly detects this mismatch (line 212). The actual issue is more subtle: nodes with in-degree zero that are not part of any cycle will be processed and removed, but if a cycle exists among nodes with initially non-zero in-degree that becomes zero only through removal of acyclic predecessors, those cycle nodes may not be identified correctly in the cycleIds filter (line 214), because the filter naively assumes all unvisited nodes are in the cycle.
evidence: src/remediate/validation/contractPipelineGates.ts:165-221 - The Kahn algorithm implementation appears correct in principle: it accumulates unvisited nodes with in-degree > 0 in cycleIds when visited < ids.size. This correctly identifies all nodes remaining in the graph when the queue empties, which must be part of a cycle.

src/remediate/validation/contractPipelineGates.ts:214 - The cycleIds calculation assumes any unvisited node must be in a cycle. However, if an obligation with id X has a typo in depends_on that references a non-existent obligation Y, then X will never be removed from the graph (its in-degree includes a dependency on Y that was filtered as external). This causes X to be falsely reported as part of a cycle when it is merely referencing a non-existent dependency.

The core issue: external dependency filtering (line 191) silently ignores depends_on entries that reference obligations not in the ledger, causing in-degrees to diverge from the actual dependency structure the caller expects.

findings.title: Token estimation does not account for provider-specific overhead; accumulated underestimate causes 429/524 errors
findings.summary: Packet sizing uses estimateTokensFromBytes (a local deterministic primitive) to estimate input/output tokens. This does not account for: (1) provider-specific prompt wrapping (each provider may add headers/footers); (2) tool-use overhead (LLM outputs tool calls, adding tokens); (3) XML tag overhead from tool inputs; (4) reasoning tokens if using extended-thinking models (P5-DR-010). A packet estimated as 50k input tokens might consume 60k+ at the actual provider. Over many packets, accumulating underestimate can exceed real TPM limits, causing 429 errors that stall dispatch. The underestimate is especially severe when packetized work includes tool-use (Read/Edit/Bash), because tool results are re-injected into the conversation, inflating actual token usage vs estimate. Dispatch then believes quota is available when in fact the next packet will exceed the limit. This is a hard limit violation waiting to happen.

findings.title: Contract pipeline and close phase should decompose into obligation chains, not monolithic functions
findings.summary: The contract pipeline (remediate/steps/contractPipeline.ts: 2,961 lines) and close phase (remediate/phases/close.ts: 1,652 lines) each handle dozens of tasks (critique gate, judge gate, test execution, build/lint, commit, push, publish) in monolithic procedural blocks. findings.title: Contract pipeline phases split into five separate files without unifying abstraction; versioning scattered
findings.summary: Remediate contract pipeline artifacts delegate to five separate phase-specific modules (goal.ts, design.ts, obligations.ts, implementation.ts, verification.ts), each defining its own contracts and version constants (CONTRACT_PIPELINE_*_SPEC_VERSION). This forces callers to import five separate version constants and track staleness across five separate files (P2-DR-004). More broadly, artifact versioning is scattered: CONTRACT_PIPELINE_* constants in five contractPipeline phase files, AUDIT_FINDINGS_* constants in audit artifact definitions, REMEDIATION_* constants in remediate, and per-phase version constants throughout (P2-DR-007). Each artifact independently tracks its own version number — a non-orthogonal design. When a breaking change affects multiple artifacts, versions must be incremented manually across multiple files, creating synchronization hazard. A cleaner design would: (1) define versioning as a first-class contract (single schema for how versions are declared/checked), (2) centralize version declarations in one authoritative location, (3) derive the version of aggregate artifacts from versions of constituent pieces, (4) make version checks deterministic and testable independent of consuming code. A simpler immediate fix: define a single versioned contract envelope wrapping all phases, with one version field that increments when ANY phase changes.

findings.title: Lock heartbeat refresh silently fails without surfacing errors to the holder
findings.summary: The lock heartbeat (fileLock.ts:191-210) runs best-effort on an interval. If utimes fails (permission error, read-only filesystem, I/O error), the failure is silently swallowed (P5-DR-011). A held lock whose heartbeat fails to refresh will eventually be classified as stale and stolen while the holder is still executing. The comment correctly identifies this as load-bearing (INV-SCC-08), but the only guard is a silent catch-all. On a system with transient I/O issues or permission problems, a holder could lose its lock mid-operation without any signal in logs. The holder would then mutate guarded files (artifact_metadata.json, state.json) concurrently with another holder, corrupting state. More correct design: escalate heartbeat failures as non-recoverable errors so the holder stops mutating and operator is aware of the problem.

findings.title: Obligation ledger stale-lock heartbeat assumes event-loop starvation < 10 seconds, unenforced
findings.summary: The file-lock heartbeat in src/shared/quota/fileLock.ts (startLockHeartbeat, line 191-210) refreshes the lock's mtime every HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL_MS (10 seconds) to prevent a live holder from being declared stale. The contract is documented as INV-SCC-08: 'Even two consecutive missed beats (event-loop stall, slow FS) leave the lock fresh.' However, this assumes event-loop stalls never exceed 20 seconds and disk I/O for timestamp touch never exceeds 10 seconds. These are operating-system assumptions with no enforcement. Under extreme load or on a slow network FS, the heartbeat could fail to run within its interval, a concurrent stealer could claim the lock, and two processes could mutate the guarded file concurrently. There's no observability (no counter or log of missed beats) to detect when this invariant is violated.

findings.title: OpenCode maintains a second copy of the loader protocol
findings.summary: The OpenCode command template independently restates the next-step loop instead of deriving from the canonical audit-code skill/prompt contract. Use `audit-code next-step` as the primary interface to the audit workflow.

1. Run `audit-code next-step` directly when shell access is available.
2. Read `prompt_content` in the response and follow it.
3. When a step completes (not blocked), run `audit-code next-step` again.
4. Stop when the step instructions say to stop.

When a step prompt tells you to continue, repeat `audit-code next-step` with the
same `--auditor` handshake and follow only the newly returned `prompt_path`. Stop
when the current step prompt tells you to stop.

findings.title: Provider dispatch silently degrades on invalid/missing host model roster; no fallback strategy
findings.summary: When the host provides an invalid --host-models JSON, parseHostModelRoster correctly throws loudly. However, if the host provides malformed or missing model roster data, the dispatch system has no fallback strategy (P5-DR-005). The scheduler depends on accurate model capabilities (context/output windows) to size packets. If windows are understated, dispatch oversizes packets against real limits, causing 429/524 errors mid-run. If windows are overstated, dispatch leaves quota on the table and wastes concurrency. A malformed roster during a long run could cause cascading failures with no clear recovery path. A more correct design would validate roster at dispatch initialization, provide sensible defaults for known models, and escalate an error with recovery instructions rather than silently proceeding with degraded signal.

findings.title: The mutation API can reject after committing data
findings.summary: mutate cannot tell its caller that the JSON replacement succeeded when lock cleanup subsequently fails: the successful persisted value remains on disk while the returned promise rejects. findings.summary: Quota handling is split across src/shared/quota, src/audit/quota, and src/remediate/quota (P2-DR-003). While per-orchestrator quota directories are thin policy wrappers (re-exporting from shared), the shared/quota directory contains many modules (limits.ts, scheduler.ts, claimRegistry.ts, modelStatics.ts, dispatchQuotaContract.ts) handling different aspects: sliding-window rate limiting, RPM/TPM parsing, model limits discovery, claim tracking. The issue is lack of orthogonality — these modules do not compose cleanly. There's a circular dependency between limits.ts and scheduler.ts (documented in P5-DR-008, P2-DR-008) suggesting abstraction boundaries are cut wrongly. The scheduler and limits should be orthogonal (scheduler decides WHEN to attempt work, limits decide HOW MUCH allowed), but instead are interdependent. A cleaner design would separate the quota model into independent layers: (1) quota ledger (raw observed consumption), (2) rate-limiting policy (exponential backoff, learned RPM/TPM ceilings), (3) work-wave scheduler (how many tasks per round). Currently they are tangled.

findings.title: Wrapper layer adds complexity and platform-specific friction; duplicates bootstrap logic and is a source of bugs
findings.summary: The audit-code wrapper (audit-code-wrapper-lib.mjs and support files) solves real problems: self-invocation for dogfooding, platform-aware spawn argument quoting for cmd.exe, detecting package-installed vs source-checked. But it adds ~500 lines of pre-dist entrypoint code that runs on EVERY invocation, duplicates bootstrap/installation logic, detects build staleness, and re-spawns the dist binary through shell quoting logic that must stay in sync with src/shared/tooling/exec.ts (P1-DR-002). For the user experience, the wrapper is invisible — they run `audit-code next-step` and it works. But maintenance cost is real: there's a parity test (wrapper-quote-parity.test.mjs) explicitly to catch drift, and the wrapper has been a source of user-facing bugs (CE-001: relative --root handled incorrectly by wrapper's cwd fork; CE-006/CE-007: flag-scanning bugs). A pragmatist would ask: does the wrapper's self-invocation convenience (dogfood uses local code, installed runs use global bin) justify the maintenance surface? Would it be cheaper to make the dist entry point aware of its own install context and drop the wrapper layer entirely? Would requiring explicit `npm run build` before `audit-code` commands (with a clear error on missing dist/) be acceptable and simpler?

findings.title: XML entity decoding order causes incorrect output for escaped sequences
findings.summary: The XML entity replacements in decodeXmlText() are applied in the wrong order. Replacing & first causes sequences like '&lt;' (which should decode to '<') to incorrectly decode to '<' instead.

affected_files.quoted_text:
function decodeXmlText(value: string): string {
  return value
    .replace(/</g, "<")
    .replace(/>/g, ">")
    .replace(/"/g, "\"")
    .replace(/'/g, "'")
    .replace(/&/g, "&");

evidence: src/audit/extractors/graphManifestEdges/maven.ts:11-18 - The sequence of replace() calls processes & first. When input is '&lt;', the & replacement converts it to '<', then < replacement converts it to '<'. Correct output should be '<' (literal text). The & replacement must occur LAST to handle escaped entities correctly.
XML entity encoding standard: entities should be decoded in reverse of encoding order, with & processed last, otherwise nested entities like &lt; decode incorrectly.

findings.title: Dependency slice projection errors silently degrade to expensive conservative comparison
findings.summary: The staleness check uses dependency-slice projections to avoid phantom-staleness when only irrelevant parts of a dependency change (P5-DR-013). When a projection throws or is unavailable, the code silently falls back to whole-artifact hash comparison. This is correct for safety but expensive: a projection that consistently errors causes the corresponding artifact to be needlessly re-computed every run, wasting quota. More critically, if a projection is registered but computation throws, there's no signal that the optimization is failing. A developer might observe degraded performance without realizing the slice projection is broken. Add instrumentation and escalation logic so projection failures are surfaced.

findings.title: Design review dispatch splits into contract + conceptual passes; seam is unclear and adds iteration cost
findings.summary: Design review runs two independent passes: (1) contract-assessment (invariants/boundaries/obligations), (2) conceptual-design-critique (philosophy/alternatives). Intent: contract issues are mechanical, conceptual critique is deeper but optional. In practice, this splits review into two separate dispatch cycles with different prompts, models, and artifact footprints. The intent is sound but the implementation cost seems high: two more stops in the 28-step chain, two more staleness dependencies (P1-DR-006). A pragmatist would ask: is this split worth the complexity? Could a single design-review prompt (with sections for contract vs conceptual) be simpler? Or, if two passes are necessary, could they be batched into one orchestrator step? The current approach adds execution complexity relative to the user-visible benefit.

findings.title: Parallelize independent analyzer runs instead of serial acquisition engine
findings.summary: The acquisitionEngine runs external analyzers sequentially (eslint, then rubocop, then semgrep, etc.). Independent analyzers (ones that don't depend on each other's output) can run in parallel. Create a ParallelAnalyzerPool that: (1) topologically sorts analyzers by dependency; (2) groups independent ones into layers; (3) issues all layer-N runs as Promise.all before proceeding to layer N+1. Example: clippy + rubocop + eslint are independent → run in parallel; then their outputs feed into the merge/deduplication step. For a typical JavaScript project with 4-6 analyzers running 2-5 seconds each, serialization costs 10-20 seconds; parallelization (3 layers of 2 each) reduces to 6-8 seconds. findings.title: Staleness cascade defeats 'only recompute when upstream changes' intent through over-broad file-change triggers
findings.summary: The staleness DAG is designed to avoid redundant recomputation — artifacts only refresh when upstream dependencies change. But implementation shows repeated friction from over-broad triggers: (1) charter-related artifacts keep WHOLE-ARTIFACT repo_manifest edges, so an unrelated manifest file-count change re-fires charter extraction (documented in open-bugs.md DD-9 entry); (2) a file rename/delete fires staleness for ANY downstream consumer even if semantic content unchanged; (3) the fixture sweep for contract changes touched tests/** and missed scripts/ producers (caught only in CI) (P1-DR-005). The system is mechanically sound but pragmatically noisy — it errs on 'recompute to be safe', which is correct but expensive. Most re-computations are (a) wasted LLM tokens on re-reading unchanged state, (b) not caught until a human observes 'this took longer than it should'. A tighter binding (per-file staleness for charter slice, content-only edits not triggering re-derivation) would reduce waste, but the cost is complexity: a more precise model requires more careful modeling of what each executor actually reads. The current 'whole-artifact is safe' approach is simpler to maintain.

findings.title: Data-drive the obligation executor registry; eliminate the executor-search pattern in decideNextStep
findings.summary: Both audit and remediate's orchestrators use a two-phase lookup: PRIORITY array lists obligations, then decideNextStep searches an executor registry to find the implementation (a linear scan or object lookup). Replace with a single, data-driven ObligationRegistry where each entry is {id, executor, phase, dependencies, priority_rank}. The registry validates at load time that every obligation has exactly one executor, no cycles exist, and phase ordering is respected. findings.title: Port remediate's artifacts to a data-driven ARTIFACT_DEFINITIONS registry like audit's, unifying IO patterns
findings.summary: Audit cleanly separates artifact IO from orchestration via ARTIFACT_DEFINITIONS (registry of {fileName, read, write} functions). findings.summary: The audit orchestrator assumes that each deterministic executor satisfies at least one obligation and never re-opens an upstream one (advance.ts:33-37). findings.title: Data-drive obligation registry instead of hardcoded PRIORITY array plus inline comments
findings.summary: Both audit (src/audit/orchestrator/nextStep.ts) and remediate obligation engines maintain a PRIORITY string[] with inline comments describing each obligation. Adding, reordering, or understanding dependencies requires reading the PRIORITY array + searching for obligation_ids in the executor registry. Replace with a data-driven registry: each obligation is a declared object { id, description, mustComeBefore: [...], executor_id, phase, category }. The registry enforces invariants (every obligation has an executor, no cycles in ordering, phase ordering respected). Benefits: dependencies are explicit + validated at load time; adding an obligation is a single structured record; the registry can emit documentation (obligation-graph.md) automatically; and violations (a removed obligation still in PRIORITY) become compile-time errors rather than silent no-op steps at runtime.

findings.title: Executor registry validation uses inefficient filter loop at module load time
findings.summary: In `src/audit/orchestrator/nextStep.ts` lines 71-84, `assertExecutorRegistryCoversPriority` validates that each obligation in PRIORITY maps to exactly one executor by filtering the entire EXECUTOR_REGISTRY for each obligation: `EXECUTOR_REGISTRY.filter((executor) => executor.obligation_ids.includes(obligationId))`. This is O(PRIORITY.length * EXECUTOR_REGISTRY.length) at module load. The code already has `EXECUTOR_BY_OBLIGATION` map at line 141; this validation could use the same map or build an inverted index for O(1) lookups. While this is a one-time module-load cost, it's inefficient and the validation logic could be cleaner.

findings.title: Extract common extractor patterns into shared base class: input validation → output normalization → staleness tracking
findings.summary: The extractors (graph.ts, disposition.ts, designAssessment.ts, risk.ts, etc.) follow an implicit pattern: (1) validate inputs are present, (2) perform extraction, (3) normalize output shape, (4) record upstream dependencies for staleness. This is re-implemented in each 10-30KB file with ~200 lines of boilerplate per extractor. Create an ExtractorPipeline<TInput, TOutput> base class that takes input-validator, extraction-fn, normalizer, and dependency-list as parameters. New extractors (or reworked existing ones) become 100-line registrations, not full modules. Benefits: uniform error handling, consistent dependency tracking, and isolation of extraction logic from plumbing.

findings.title: Test suite size and complexity inversely correlates with iteration speed; comprehensive but potentially over-scoped
findings.summary: The codebase has 1076 TypeScript files (per audit context), with a large test suite covering audit-code, remediate-code, and shared. The suite is comprehensive and has caught real bugs (P1-DR-010). But pragmatically, this size has costs: (1) test runs are slow, making tight iteration cycles hard; (2) every code change requires updating multiple test fixtures and contracts; (3) contract changes sweep hundreds of test files, creating churn; (4) new engineers take time to understand which tests cover which code paths. A pragmatist might ask: is 1076 files the right scope, or has the test suite grown beyond marginal value? Are there tests that could be consolidated (five similar dispatch-scenario tests → one parametrized suite)? Are there integration-test coverage gaps not worth filling? This is not a suggestion to cut testing — the project benefits from thorough testing — but rather to be intentional about test scope. The current approach seems 'comprehensive coverage is always better', which is safe but not pragmatic when tight iteration speed matters.

findings.title: cross-lens-dedup.test.ts: Good defensive testing but missing mutation of source evidence arrays
findings.summary: Tests verify that source findings' affected_files, summary, and evidence arrays are NOT mutated by deduplication (lines 349-450). This is excellent defensive testing. However, the tests do NOT verify that the source evidence array reference itself is not mutated (a potential vector if evidence is deep-copied but the array object reference is shared).
evidence: tests/remediate/cross-lens-dedup.test.ts:384 - assertion 'expect(absorbed.evidence).toEqual(originalEvidence)' verifies content equality but does not assert that absorbed.evidence is still the same array reference (originalEvidence === absorbed.evidence). A shallow copy attack on the evidence array would pass this test.

tests/remediate/cross-lens-dedup.test.ts:350-374 - affected_files mutation test uses 'expect(original.affected_files).toBe(originalFilesRef)' (line 371) to verify reference equality. The evidence test should do the same for consistency and to catch shallow copy attacks.

themes.title: Concurrent State & Artifact Validation
themes.root_cause: Multiple concurrent orchestrator runs share mutable artifacts with weak synchronization; file locks lack staleness detection, schema versioning is uncentralized, and artifact reads bypass validation entirely. This creates data corruption risks where Run A and Run B can simultaneously hold different locks and silently overwrite each other's findings, or produce findings from stale metadata.
themes.suggested_fix_pattern: Centralize staleness derivation and artifact versioning in shared as a single ArtifactRegistry; enforce explicit schema validation on all artifact reads before use; unify lock heartbeat and timeout mechanics with explicit timeout-margin validation; make concurrent write ordering deterministic (one-at-a-time serialization or explicit version-compare-and-swap) rather than best-effort.

themes.title: Type Safety & Correctness Gaps
themes.root_cause: Runtime type mismatches and incorrect algorithm implementations create silent failures and state corruption: type-unsafe validation, case-sensitive checks that fail on Windows, regex false-positives, wrong return values in critical functions, and missing bounds checks. These are fixable with stronger types and deterministic validation, but currently spread across ~50 locations with no unified guard.
themes.suggested_fix_pattern: Upgrade TypeScript strictness and validation on all input types; add property-based tests for edge cases (empty arrays, case sensitivity, regex boundaries); extract validation predicates to a single shared module; use zod or similar for deterministic schema enforcement at every I/O boundary; enforce bounds checks before array access.

themes.title: Monolithic Orchestrators & Implicit Control Flow
themes.root_cause: The audit orchestrator (28-obligation priority chain) and remediate orchestrator (5600+ line nextStep) are too large and complex for single-person understanding. Control flow is implicit (drain-fold-halt model never documented), state machines are embedded in conditionals, obligation engine and executor coupling is dual-sourced and manually kept in sync. This friction makes feature development expensive and bugs hard to debug.
themes.suggested_fix_pattern: Decompose each orchestrator into: (1) a thin dispatcher/phase-machine that scans priorities and routes to phase executors; (2) separate phase modules (planning, implementing, closing, etc.) with explicit state machines as data (not conditionals); (3) document the obligation engine and drain-fold-halt semantics in code; (4) add an ARCHITECTURE.md guide that explains the pipeline and critical files in read order for new developers.

themes.title: Error Handling & Silent Failures
themes.root_cause: Critical code paths silently degrade or drop errors: external analyzer acquisition returns empty results when tools are unavailable, packet validation doesn't reject malformed JSON, cooldown handling loses quota context, lock heartbeats fail without surfacing errors, and resource leaks are common (unreleased claims, uncleaned temp dirs). The tool is designed to fail-closed, but the result is invisible degradation and quota burnout.
themes.suggested_fix_pattern: Add explicit logging at every error boundary; distinguish between transient (retry) and fatal (escalate) errors; validate packet schema eagerly before persisting; use try/finally for all resource cleanup; escalate degradation (missing tools, failed quota probes) to the run summary so it is visible; add timeouts to all I/O operations that can hang; wrap Promise.all writes with explicit error recovery or atomicity enforcement.

themes.title: Code Duplication & Missing Shared Infrastructure
themes.root_cause: Identical logic is implemented in multiple files (validator patterns, fixture builders, tree walkers, tool-execution handlers, formatter loops) creating maintenance burden and silent drift. Additionally, shared infrastructure that should be centralized (audit and remediate both have independent quota/providers wiring, staleness logic differs between orchestrators) is duplicated instead of unified.
themes.suggested_fix_pattern: Extract duplicated validators, helpers, and fixture builders to a single shared location; create shared test-helpers module for common Finding/State builders; unify staleness derivation in an ArtifactRegistry owned by shared; wrap circular dependencies by moving the upstream concept into shared; audit/remediate should import not duplicate orchestration logic.

themes.title: Test Coverage Gaps in Critical Paths
themes.root_cause: Approximately 45+ findings indicate missing or incomplete test coverage in critical modules: content-key derivation, path-identity normalization, scheduler logic, provider diagnostics, contract-pipeline derivation, and high-complexity functions lack dedicated unit tests. Drift guards exist (e.g., stableStringify duplication) but the real defect (the duplication) persists because single-source extraction is not enforced mechanically.
themes.suggested_fix_pattern: Add unit tests for every shared export (content-key, path-identity, scheduler, quota logic); move drift-guard tests from individual test files to central shared tests; add integration tests that exercise the production result boundary (F3 tests should drive real rolling-dispatch); increase coverage target from 45% to 75%+ for shared and orchestrator code.

themes.title: Provider Dispatch Routing is Implicit & Complex
themes.root_cause: Provider selection logic stratifies across five layers (auto-detection, capability matching, quota tier selection, learned limits, fallover) with orthogonal concerns mixed in a single priority sequence. Rules are applied independently by callers (dozens of places), no central registry determines regenerability vs costliness of artifacts, and audit/remediate duplicate dispatch logic independently. When routing fails, debugging is hard because the decision scatters across files and layers.
themes.suggested_fix_pattern: Create a unified DispatchRouter in shared that centralizes all routing decisions (provider selection, capability matching, quota tier bucketing, learned limits, failover); expose a single entry point with explicit input/output contracts; make the priority rules explicit as data (not conditionals); centralize regenerability categorization in the ArtifactRegistry; merge audit and remediate dispatch logic into one implementation owned by shared.

themes.title: Security & Authorization Gaps
themes.root_cause: Several security boundaries are weak or missing: no validation of path parameters (risk: path traversal), OAuth tokens written without restrictive file modes (risk: credential exposure), quota metadata interpolated into prompts without escaping (risk: prompt injection), and remediation write-scope fails open when plan reads fail (risk: authorization bypass).
themes.suggested_fix_pattern: Add input validation for all path parameters; use explicit restrictive file modes (0600) when writing credentials; escape all dynamic data before interpolating into prompts; validate write-scope plans eagerly and fail closed (deny all) when unreadable; add a security review gate to pre-commit for credential-handling code.

themes.title: Deterministic Graph Extraction Produces Unvalidated Leads
themes.root_cause: The audit pipeline extracts dependency graphs deterministically (ast-grep, tree-sitter, manifest parsers) but this output is LEADS, not verdicts. However, graph-derived findings (test/asset/manifest edges, co-change counts, file co-mentions) are promoted to findings without semantic confirmation or explicit semantic boundary checks. This produces noisy, low-actionability findings.
themes.suggested_fix_pattern: Exclude test/asset/manifest edges from the starting graph, or require explicit semantic confirmation (documented risk reason, interdependency documentation) before promotion to findings; add a post-extraction semantic review gate that confirms high-confidence graph changes before reporting; stratify findings by provenance (deterministic extraction vs LLM-confirmed vs manual review).

themes.title: Missing Observability & Distributed Tracing
themes.root_cause: Critical paths lack logging or trace context: dispatch pause lifecycle is silent, contract-pipeline derivations have no request IDs, critical deployment/rollback events are not logged, and error conditions in external tool acquisition are invisible. This makes operational debugging impossible.
themes.suggested_fix_pattern: Add structured logging at every critical transition (phase changes, dispatch decisions, error conditions); add trace/request IDs to contract-pipeline derivations; make run degradation visible in the audit report (indicate which analyzers were skipped, which quota sources were unavailable); add a deployment smoke test that verifies configuration is isolated and does not touch the operator's real home.

executive_summary: This 2,179-finding audit of audit-tools reveals three categories of defects. First, concurrent state management and artifact validation are fragile: file locks are weak, schema versioning is uncentralized, and runs can silently corrupt shared artifacts. Second, type safety gaps and algorithm errors are scattered across ~50 locations (case sensitivity bugs, type mismatches, wrong return values) with no unified guard — these are fixable with stronger validation but currently spread and untracked. Third, the orchestrators have grown monolithic (28-obligation chain, 5600-line nextStep) with implicit control flow that makes feature development expensive. Duplication is endemic (identical validators, fixture builders, dispatch logic in both orchestrators), error handling is silent (no logging, no escalation), and test coverage gaps are large (45+ findings for critical untested paths). The tool is designed correctly in principle but complexity has accumulated without refactoring; the fixes are architectural carving (decompose orchestrators, unify shared infrastructure, centralize routing) rather than localized patches.
top_risks: Concurrent orchestrator runs can silently corrupt shared findings artifacts via race conditions in file locking and metadata versioning (DAT-d3d6f01b, REL-d3d6f01b)
Type-unsafe validation and algorithm errors (50+ findings) create runtime crashes and silent data corruption with no centralized guard
Monolithic orchestrators (5600+ line functions) hide control flow and make feature development expensive; the 28-obligation priority chain has high friction for capability changes
Silent error degradation (missing tools, failed quota probes, resource leaks) makes runs proceed with degraded signal and no visibility to operators
Test coverage gaps in critical paths (content-key, path-identity, scheduler, quota logic) leave high-confidence bugs undetected until production
Provider dispatch routing is implicit across five layers with duplicate logic in audit/remediate; when routing fails, debugging is hard and changes affect both orchestrators unpredictably

Security boundaries are weak: no path validation (traversal risk), weak file modes on credentials (exposure risk), prompt injection risk in quota metadata, authorization bypass when write-scope plan fails
